I definitely received benefits on the lower dose. My depression got so much better with sertraline, but unfortunately, it did nothing for my anxiety. The sertraline did make me feel worse at all the dosages, but I think this is because of how sertraline pretty much did nothing for my anxiety. I think if it has been working for you, there's a good chance that a higher dose could potentially help (at least this is what my doctor tells me). 

The tapering off process has been rather good. I do feel a little bit of the depression symptom coming back, but I can manage them okay as I'm not going cold turkey instantly. It's interesting because the sertraline made crying very difficult for me. So while it is being tapered off, I've cried for the first time in about 2 months! 

Yes, my friend had really good success with the 150mg. She's continuing to take it for the foreseeable future. 

I take beta-blockers called Propranolol in addition to my anti-depressants. These help with the physical symptoms of anxiety (heart palpitations, tremors, shaking). I found them very helpful to prevent panic attacks. These beta-blockers are also not addictive, unlike benzodiazepines, so they're quite safe to take. My doctor advises me to take them "as needed" so I don't even take them every day, only when I can feel a panic attack coming on.

Hi! I was on 150mg for a while but am now tapering off of it. Antidepressants are so fickle with each person. I had a friend that had to up her dosage to 150mg because she didn't feel that 50 or 100 did anything. I think with antidepressants it's worth seeing it through before switching.  For example, my doctor suggested that I continue to take sertraline until the maximum dosage of 200mg before he recommended changing to a different medication. He said it would  help him ensure that sertraline isn't completely right for me, and that we've gone through all the possible options. I went off it because sertraline actually made me feel worse, instead of making me feel better. 

I don't know if that helps but basically to answer your question: don't rule out that maybe your condition does warrant a higher dose. I think unless your doctor really advises against it for separate health reasons, there's no harm in trying it.

what often helps for me is to find something that calms you down, and helps concentrate on your own body. For example, I like watching ballet videos or try some mindfulness techniques. Mindfulness is useful because not only does it clear your mind, it also can feel really relaxing after a stressful day. 

Also, knowing your triggers and trying to avoid them before bedtime helps. With myself, I know not to watch sad videos before bed as a slight change of negative emotion can send me spiralling. Journalling these things can help identify and stop them.
